title: Decision-curve prioritization with risk-weighted RICE for latency/cost uncertainty
creator: Samantha Li
description:
Background: We need a prioritization framework that transparently combines expected user value with the uncertainty (variance) in latency and per-token cost impact. Traditional RICE (Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort) gives a point estimate but hides risk from latency spikes and cost volatility, which matter for inference services.

Problem: Several candidate initiatives (e.g., kernel-autotuner, prefix-cache rewrite, batching policy overhaul) score similarly on static RICE but have very different tail risk profiles: some increase 95th-percentile latency under load or require uncertain infra spend. Product and Eng lack a simple decision tool that surfaces these trade-offs and lets PMs pick features aligned with risk tolerance and SLOs.

Goal: Deliver a decision-curve prioritization artefact and lightweight calculator/Playbook that: (1) augments RICE with latency/cost uncertainty, (2) outputs a ranked list of initiatives under different risk tolerances, and (3) is simple enough for quarter planning and exec trade-off conversations.
proposal:
Introduce a risk-weighted RICE variant that replaces a single Confidence scalar with a Monte Carlo-derived distribution over net expected value (NEV). NEV = (Estimated Revenue Uplift * Reach * Impact) - Expected Additional Cost. For each initiative we model uncertainty in latency and cost as simple distributions (triangular or log-normal) informed by eng estimates and historical kernel rollouts. We run N=2000 samples and compute: expected NEV, probability NEV<0, expected 95th-pct latency, and probability(95th>latency_SLO). The core output is a decision curve: x-axis = risk tolerance (max acceptable P(95th>SLO)), y-axis = subset of initiatives with highest expected NEV under that tolerance.

Practicalities: keep inputs minimal so PMs can fill in a spreadsheet quickly: reach, impact_scale (1-5), base_cost_estimate, cost_volatility_pct, base_latency_delta_ms, latency_volatility_pct, effort_points. Provide default priors derived from recent infra experiments. Create a Google Sheets + Python notebook that executes sampling for transparency and reproducibility.
scoring_model_details:
Formula summary: For each sim draw i: revenue_i = baseline_revenue * reach * impact_scale * uplift_draw; cost_i = base_cost_estimate * (1 + cost_noise_draw); latency_i = baseline_95th + latency_delta_draw. NEV_i = revenue_i - cost_i - effort_point_cost. Output metrics: expected_NEV = mean(NEV_i), downside_prob = P(NEV_i<0), latency_tail = quantile(latency_i, 0.95), slo_breach_prob = P(latency_i>latency_SLO). Risk-adjusted score = expected_NEV * (1 - alpha * slo_breach_prob) where alpha is risk_penalty (0.0–1.0) set by PM/exec.

We recommend two default modes: conservative (alpha=0.9) and growth (alpha=0.2).
example_calculation:
Example: Kernel Autotuner (estimates): reach=0.2 (20% of traffic), impact=0.3, baseline_revenue="$4M/yr" for product surface, uplift_draw ~ Normal(0.03,0.01), base_cost_estimate="$120k/yr", cost_volatility=20%, base_latency=60ms, latency_delta=-5ms mean (sd 8ms). Monte Carlo (N=2000) -> expected_NEV="$320k", downside_prob=12%, slo_breach_prob=3%. Growth mode rank: top-3. Conservative mode (alpha=0.9) deprioritizes it due to downside_prob >10% depending on SLO.

This illustrative calc and assumptions are captured in the shared sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/decision-curve-prioritization (internal) and notebook: https://github.com/redwood-inference/prioritization/decision-curves
acceptance_criteria:
1) Publish prioritization Playbook document and shared Google Sheets template.
2) Deliver reference implementation (Python notebook + simple Flask UI) that ingests CSV of initiatives and outputs ranked lists for at least two risk modes.
3) Run the model with Q2 candidate initiatives and present results at Roadmap review.
4) Collect feedback from at least 3 Eng leads and 2 Design/PM partners and iterate.
5) Documentation includes clear input defaults, interpretation guidance, and example calculations.

risks: Model complexity vs adoption: too many inputs will reduce use — mitigated by conservative defaults. Data quality: priors may be wrong for novel work. SLO misalignment: decision curves depend on correct SLO selection. Exec acceptance: need one clear example where this changes the rank vs static RICE.
